title: A small rebound in media confidence does not undo historically weak and partisan trust
source_unit: Gallup Governance poll and long-run U.S. media-confidence trend

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in Gallup Governance poll; public article does not state the sample size

media_confidence.unit: percent expressing a great deal or fair amount of confidence in newspapers, television and radio to report news fully, accurately and fairly

limited_or_no_confidence.unit: percent expressing not very much or no confidence

year_over_year_rebound.value: confidence rose from 28% in 2025, but remains near the bottom of Gallup's more than 50-year trend

rebound_without_restoration.value: A year-over-year improvement can be real without representing institutional recovery when the majority still lacks confidence.

observations.method: Gallup Governance poll conducted September 1-17, 2026, reported alongside Gallup's long-run media-confidence trend; the public article does not state the sample size or full sampling details.
observations.uncertainty: The survey predates major White House-media-access events beginning September 18; the article cautions that any effect of those events is not reflected. Confidence is reported perception, not a content-accuracy audit or news-use measure.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults; party identification is reported separately.
observations.counterinterpretation: The rebound may reflect changing political evaluations, event salience or sampling variation rather than broad restoration of journalistic credibility.

observations.period: September 1-17, 2026; partisan divergence in media confidence

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in Gallup Governance poll; party subgroup denominators not disclosed in public article

republican_confidence.unit: percent of Republicans expressing confidence, up from 8% in 2025

democratic_confidence.unit: percent of Democrats expressing confidence, versus 51% in 2025

partisan_authority_gap.value: The same information institution is evaluated through sharply different partisan trust channels, leaving shared public facts vulnerable to identity-based filtering.

observations.method: Gallup subgroup estimates from the September 2026 Governance poll and historical trend comparison.
observations.uncertainty: The release does not identify the causes of partisan movement, exposure patterns, outlet mix, ideological composition, or whether confidence predicts use, sharing, correction acceptance or civic action.
observations.subgroup: Republicans, Democrats and independents in the U.S. adult sample.
observations.counterinterpretation: Partisan confidence may track changing evaluations of media coverage rather than fixed hostility to news institutions; trust in particular outlets can differ from trust in mass media overall.

denominator.unit: Gallup historical trend series; public article does not provide a single pooled denominator

historical_high.value: about seven in ten in the 1970s, above 50% through the early 2000s

current_low.value: confidence fell below 30% for the first time in 2025 and is 33% in 2026

institutional_memory.value: Trust is shaped by accumulated political conflict and repeated credibility disputes, not only the current news cycle.

open_conversion.value: The unresolved stage is whether stronger reporting, transparency, correction and plural source ecosystems can convert episodic confidence movement into durable legitimacy.

observations.method: Historical comparisons summarized by Gallup from its more than 50-year media-confidence trend.
observations.uncertainty: Historical question wording, modes, samples and media environments change over time; the trend does not identify a single causal driver or establish that the current measure is comparable in every respect across decades.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults across historical survey periods.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low confidence in mass media may coexist with trust in particular journalists, local outlets, public broadcasters, specialized sources or interpersonal verification networks.

related_sources.claim: Official Gallup article reports current media confidence, partisan comparisons, field dates, event-timing boundary and historical trend.

boundary: This record adds a media-legitimacy route from long-run confidence decline through partisan divergence, event-sensitive rebound and possible source-selection or civic consequences. It does not measure news accuracy, exposure, outlet-level trust, sharing, correction, misinformation, causal political behavior or the effect of post-fieldwork events.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Gallup article was reviewed for the 2026 confidence estimate, 2025 comparison, partisan subgroup estimates, September 1-17 field period, post-fieldwork event boundary and historical trend framing.
